policy: No AI-generated imagery. Object-level rights and the named institution's record govern.

objects.title: Dress
objects.caption: A garment record becomes institutional evidence when material, date, maker, identifier, and rights remain attached.
objects.alt: Eighteenth-century French silk dress with a fitted bodice and full skirt, from The Metropolitan Museum of Art collection.

objects.title: Afternoon dress
objects.credit: Brooklyn Museum Costume Collection at The Metropolitan Museum of Art; Gift of Marion Litchfield, 1950
objects.caption: A less-remembered house remains researchable because its object record survives.
objects.alt: Pale silk afternoon dress by Jeanne Hallée, shown from the front at a three-quarter angle.

objects.title: Dress
objects.credit: Gift of Miss Eva Drexel Dahlgren, 1976
objects.caption: Construction evidence can outlive the operating house—but only if the physical object and record stay paired.
objects.alt: Light-colored linen and cotton dress dated around 1903, displayed frontally.

objects.title: Ball gown
objects.credit: Gift of Mrs. Philip K. Rhinelander, 1946
objects.caption: The house is visible as both maker attribution and an enduring cataloguing unit.
objects.alt: Elaborately trimmed silk ball gown by the House of Worth, dated around 1872.

objects.title: Liz Claiborne, fashion designer, with model
objects.credit: Bernard Gotfryd photograph collection, Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division
objects.caption: One frame holds a named designer, a model, a photographer, a collection, and an institutional record—separate roles that public shorthand often compresses.
objects.alt: Fashion designer Liz Claiborne standing beside a model in a Library of Congress photograph by Bernard Gotfryd.
objects.license: Free to Use and Reuse / Library of Congress curated set

objects.title: Sporting Look, evening fashions
objects.credit: Toni Frissell Collection, Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division
objects.caption: The image is a distinct authored work around fashion; the clothes, staging, model, commission, publication, and photograph do not collapse into one ownership question.
objects.alt: Two models wearing evening fashions in a 1956 Toni Frissell photograph made for Sports Illustrated.
objects.license: Free to Use and Reuse / Library of Congress curated set

objects.title: Report of New York fashions, spring and summer 1872
objects.credit: Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division
objects.caption: The sheet demonstrates a contract-shaped network of design, printing, manufacture, advertising, attribution, and distribution—even when the operative agreements are absent from the image.
objects.alt: A color advertising lithograph presenting Butterick and Company New York fashions for spring and summer 1872.
objects.license: Free to Use and Reuse / Library of Congress curated set

objects.title: S.D. Sollers & Co., manufacturers of children's fine shoes
objects.credit: Popular Graphic Arts Collection, Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division
objects.caption: A commercial name can identify the business presented to buyers while the image itself preserves a different maker attribution.
objects.alt: An 1874 illustrated advertisement for S.D. Sollers and Company children's shoes, lithographed by Duval and Hunter.
objects.license: Free to Use and Reuse / Library of Congress curated set

objects.title: Evening dress
objects.credit: Brooklyn Museum Costume Collection at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of the Brooklyn Museum, 2009; Gift of the Princess Viggo in accordance with the wishes of the Misses Hewitt, 1931
objects.caption: The record separates the material dress, House of Worth attribution, Charles Frederick Worth design credit, accession, and the museum’s present custody.
objects.alt: Ivory and blue silk evening dress with a fitted bodice, deep neckline, and long trained skirt, designed by Charles Frederick Worth around 1882.

objects.title: Ball gown
objects.maker: House of Worth; attributed to Charles Frederick Worth and Jean-Philippe Worth
objects.credit: Brooklyn Museum Costume Collection at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of the Brooklyn Museum, 2009; Gift of Mrs. C. Oliver Iselin, 1961
objects.caption: The dual designer attribution makes succession visible as an evidence question: house continuity does not erase uncertainty about individual authorship.
objects.alt: Ornate pale silk House of Worth ball gown with floral decoration and a full trained skirt, dated 1895 to 1900.

objects.title: Fancy dress costume
objects.credit: Gift of James A. and Mary Elizabeth Kingsland, 1994
objects.caption: An accession-quality record preserves a house object beyond the founder’s lifetime while keeping the object, maker attribution, and museum stewardship distinct.
objects.alt: Elaborate House of Worth silk fancy dress costume with a fitted bodice, dark patterned skirt, and dramatic decorative sleeves, around 1893.

objects.title: Evening dress
objects.credit: Gift of Miss Eva Drexel Dahlgren, 1976
objects.caption: Made after Charles Frederick Worth’s death, the dress lets the house name continue in the record without proving who controlled every creative or economic decision.
objects.alt: House of Worth silk evening dress from 1898 to 1900 with a pale embellished bodice, narrow waist, and richly patterned trained skirt.

objects.title: Gloria Vanderbilt Cooper
objects.credit: Toni Frissell Collection, Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division
objects.caption: The frame is not neutral delivery: pose, setting, crop, light, garment, commission, and publication context combine to manufacture a public fashion meaning.
objects.alt: Gloria Vanderbilt Cooper photographed by Toni Frissell for Vogue in 1966.
objects.license: Free to Use and Reuse / Library of Congress curated set

objects.title: Ball gown
objects.caption: Materials such as silk, glass, and metallic thread make skilled transformation visible while the museum record still names only the house as maker.
objects.alt: House of Worth ball gown from about 1887, with a structured pale silk silhouette and elaborate surface ornament.

objects.title: Walking suit
objects.credit: Brooklyn Museum Costume Collection at The Metropolitan Museum of Art; Gift of the Princess Viggo in accordance with the wishes of the Misses Hewitt, 1931
objects.caption: A finished suit can preserve the house name while leaving the cutters, fitters, stitchers, finishers, and production negotiations unnamed.
objects.alt: Dark silk House of Worth walking suit from about 1889, photographed frontally against a neutral background.

objects.title: Ensemble
objects.credit: Brooklyn Museum Costume Collection at The Metropolitan Museum of Art; Gift of Edith Gardiner, 1926
objects.caption: The ensemble carries material decisions across components; the surviving object cannot narrate every demonstration, correction, and embodied judgment that produced them.
objects.alt: House of Worth ensemble from 1893 in dark silk with jet and metal ornament, shown frontally.
